blocks.text: British Columbia·New

The study showed 47 per cent of B.C. women reported experiencing intimate partner violence. That figure, calculated from 2025 data, has held steady since the last report, which examined numbers gathered in 2018.
New Statistics Canada numbers show nationwide bump in reports from young women
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 19, 2026 4:39 PM EST | Last Updated: 21 minutes ago
Almost half of women in B.C. have reported experiencing intimate partner violence at least once since the age of 15, according to a new Statistics Canada report released on Wednesday.
In the study, intimate partner violence is defined as psychological, physical and sexual abuse. It can range from name-calling and manipulation to physical and sexual assault.
Nationwide, 45.1 per cent of women reported intimate partner violence, up from 44 per cent.
The study is based on the 2025 Survey of Safety in Public and Private Spaces, which was administered both online and via the telephone, and included over 46,500 respondents in the 10 provinces.
The study found that across the country, more younger women — aged 15 to 24 years old — are reporting intimate partner violence. (khuncho007/Shutterstock)
Younger women reporting more
At the same time, the study found that across the country, more younger women — aged 15 to 24 years old — are reporting intimate partner violence.
That number has bumped up to 58.5 per cent, up from 55.75 per cent.
Angela Marie MacDougall, executive director of Battered Women's Support Services, said the uptick may be the result of an increased willingness to report — a change from previous generations.
"The time of where survivors, victims, didn't report, they just had to deal with it like my mother and my grandmother," said MacDougall of what those previous generations went through.

Angela Marie MacDougall, executive director of Battered Women's Support Services, says the increases may be the result of an increased willingness to report — a change from previous generations. (CBC)
She said a greater willingness to report also comes at a time when there have been regressions in women's rights.
"There's more of a push back within the culture against the forces that would want to entrench violence against women," said MacDougall.
She said accountability work from community organizations and media is making victims feel like reporting intimate partner violence will create a meaningful result.

blocks.text: "It's more like if I report, I have a better chance of having a result that is going to help me be safer," said MacDougall.
She said her organization has seen an 80 per cent increase in requests for services since the same time last year.
Racialized women less likely to report: worker

The new Statistics Canada numbers also show that racialized women — defined in the report as those who are not white and not Indigenous — are reporting intimate partner violence at a lower rate than their white counterparts.
About 29.4 per cent of racialized women reported having experienced intimate partner violence at least once since the age of 15.
This number was 48.7 per cent for non-racialized women.
Syma Nehal of Nisa Homes says she's seen first-hand why immigrant women are often the most reluctant to report intimate partner violence. (Bismah Mughal/CBC)
But Syma Nehal said this doesn't show the full picture.
She works directly with immigrant women at Nisa Homes, which provides transitional housing for women fleeing intimate partner violence.
Nehal said she's seen first-hand why immigrant women are often the most reluctant to report.
"They're unfamiliar with systems … or they're isolated from their communities," said Nehal. "And so some of these abusers will exploit those fears by threatening deportation."

She said there is a lack of effort to recognize the unique cultural barriers these women face, which is why progress on making it safe for women to report intimate partner violence is still slow, even as immigration continues to grow.
